title: Heartbeat and cron
description: How an agent lives without your messages: schedules, background wake-ups and the right to stay quiet.

steps.question: Can an agent write to you first, without a message from you?
steps.answer: It can: a schedule wakes it up. But it only speaks up if there is a reason. Otherwise it stays quiet. That is a heartbeat.

steps.text: Cron is a scheduler from 1970s Unix: “run this command on a schedule.” A report every day at 9:00, a check every 15 minutes. The schedule is fixed and so is the action. That is perfect for reminders: “at 6 pm, show a push notification: call Mom.”

steps.imagePrompt: Night scene: a small robot resting on a phone screen wakes up to a softly pulsing heartbeat line and an old alarm clock, and thoughtfully checks whether there is anything worth telling its sleeping owner.
steps.caption: The agent wakes up on a schedule, and may stay quiet

steps.text: A heartbeat comes from server monitoring: a system regularly sends a sign that it is alive. Agents use the same idea in a new way. A schedule wakes the agent itself, and the agent DECIDES whether there is a reason to bother you. The schedule is fixed, but the action is up to the agent.

steps.definition: After a scheduled wake-up, the agent looks at the data. If there is no reason to act, it replies with the service word HEARTBEAT_OK, and you see nothing.
steps.example: A night check of your tasks: everything is fine → HEARTBEAT_OK → not a single push. Without this, a proactive agent is a spammer.

steps.caption: Run the day and move the slider. The schedule and the deadline are just an example; on Android a heartbeat runs at most once every 15 minutes

steps.text: Android has its own rules: the system strictly limits what an app can do in the background. Our version of cron is WorkManager. It guarantees that the task will run, but not at the exact minute (the system saves battery, and doze mode can delay a run). Periodic tasks run at most once every 15 minutes.

And a word about cost: every wake-up is a real model call, sometimes with tools. So a background turn has a limit on loops and fewer tools than usual. It can read data, write to memory and send notifications. It cannot delete anything, send anything outside the app, or create new heartbeats. There is nobody there to ask for your “OK,” so anything risky is simply forbidden.

steps.instruction: Match each mechanism to what it is:

pairs.def: A fixed schedule with a preset action
Wakes the agent; the agent decides what to do
Android's scheduler: it will run the task, but not at an exact minute

steps.situation: A heartbeat wakes the agent at night. The tasks are on track, the budget is fine and there are no deadlines.
options: Reply HEARTBEAT_OK and stay quiet: no reason to act
Send a push saying “all is well” to put your mind at ease
Invent a task for itself, since it is awake anyway
steps.explain: The right to stay quiet: a push without a reason is spam. It woke up, checked, and said nothing.

steps.text: Practice. Try it live after the lesson. Open the “Task list” agent. It keeps your tasks in its own memory and can see them when it wakes up. Add a couple of tasks and say: “set a heartbeat every 30 minutes, with no separate task. You decide whether there is anything to tell me.” You will see a card with the schedule and a cancel button. When the agent wakes up, it looks at your tasks: if there is a reason, you get a push, and if not, it stays quiet. Don't forget to cancel it afterwards if it was just a test :)

In short. Cron is a fixed schedule with a preset action. A heartbeat is a schedule that wakes the agent, and the agent decides, all the way down to “stay quiet” (HEARTBEAT_OK). On Android, WorkManager handles this: at most once every 15 minutes, with no promise of an exact minute. Every wake-up is a real model call, so it has a loop limit and fewer tools: no deleting and no sending anything outside the app.

questions.q: How is an agent's heartbeat different from classic cron?
options: Cron runs a fixed action on a schedule; a heartbeat wakes the agent, and the agent decides what to do
A heartbeat is just a more frequent cron: shorter intervals, but the action is still fixed
Cron was made for servers and stayed there, while a heartbeat only applies to mobile apps
questions.explain: Both have a fixed schedule. The difference is the action: with cron it is set in advance, with a heartbeat the agent itself decides, all the way down to “stay quiet.”

questions.q: Why does an agent reply HEARTBEAT_OK?
options: It is a technical signal that the LLM is still alive and answering scheduled calls
It means “all is well, no need to bother the user,” so no notification is shown
It asks the system to extend the agent's loop limit for the next wake-up
questions.explain: The right to stay quiet is what separates a polite proactive agent from a spammer: it woke up, but it did not bother you.

questions.q: Why can't a periodic heartbeat on Android run every 5 minutes?
options: An LLM usually can't return an answer within five minutes, so calls pile up in a queue
WorkManager allows periodic tasks at most once every 15 minutes, to protect the battery
The device's memory can't handle writes that often and starts losing some data
questions.explain: 15 minutes is WorkManager's hard limit for periodic tasks. On top of that, doze mode can delay a run even more.
